t0_0.desc: Measures load performance of the largest image or text block. Target: < 2.5s. Key causes: slow server, render-blocking resources, slow resource load, client-side rendering.
t0_0.what:
Definition: Largest Contentful Paint indicates how quickly the user sees the page’s main content — usually the hero image or a large heading. Good: ≤2.5s, poor: >4s (at the 75th percentile).

LCP breaks into four parts: TTFB, resource load delay, resource load duration, element render delay. First check which part is largest.
t0_0.why: This is the metric closest to the user’s “page has loaded” feeling and also an SEO ranking signal. Optimizing the wrong area (e.g., compressing images when the problem is late discovery) doesn’t change anything.
pros: Directly connected to user-perceived load speed
cons: Depends on server, network, and rendering — root cause must be identified
gotchas: Adding loading="lazy" to the LCP image is the most common mistake
Browsers discover CSS background images late — use <img> or preload instead
In client-side rendered apps, LCP occurs only after JavaScript
terms: When the largest image/text block in the viewport was rendered. Target ≤ 2.5s.
LCP = sum of server response, resource discovery, download, and render delay.
With fetchpriority="high" the browser fetches the LCP image first.
where: The hero image or heading is the LCP.
Search Console Core Web Vitals report.

t0_1.what: Definition: Measures the time from an interaction (click/tap/keypress) to the next paint when the screen updates. It replaced FID in 2024 because FID only measured the first interaction and only the delay.
t0_1.why: If the main thread is busy (large JS, hydration, heavy re-render), the UI stalls after a button click. When INP is poor, the site feels laggy even if the load is fast.
cons: Difficult to reproduce in lab; requires field data (RUM)
gotchas: Third-party scripts also block the main thread
Even a small handler can be slow because of a large re-render
INP looks at interactions across the page’s entire lifetime, not just load
terms: Approximately the slowest (p98) interaction latency among all page interactions. Target ≤ 200 ms.
Work on the main thread longer than 50 ms — blocks input handling.
The three phases of INP: wait before the handler, handler execution time, and time until the next paint.

t0_2.what:
Definition: CLS impact fraction × distance fraction is formed. Shifts that occur within 500 ms of a user click are not counted (they are expected).

Common causes: images without dimensions, late-loading ads/banners, font swap, dynamically injected content above.
t0_2.why: If the layout moves while pressing a button, the wrong item gets clicked. CLS affects both user trust and conversions.
pros: Fix is often a simple CSS/markup change.
cons: Debugging late dynamic content is a bit tricky.
gotchas: Shifts can still be counted after a bfcache restore.
Insert content below or in a reserved slot instead of above.
Font swap also creates CLS.
terms: Cumulative score of unexpected layout shifts. Target ≤ 0.1.
A visible element changes position without user input.
Provide width, height, or aspect-ratio in advance for images/ads/embeds.

t0_3.what: Definition: First Contentful Paint is the first moment when anything (non-white) appears on the page. It depends on TTFB and render-blocking resources.
t0_3.why: The user needs feedback that something is happening. If FCP is fast, bounce rate decreases, even if the full content arrives later.
cons: FCP alone does not tell the whole user experience story
gotchas: A spinner after a blank white screen can also be counted as FCP
The larger the CSS, the later the FCP
Invisible text due to fonts can delay FCP
terms: First content pixel (text/image) appears. Target ≤ 1.8 s.
Paint is paused until the head's CSS/synchronous JS loads.
If FCP is poor, LCP will also be poor.
where: FCP comes from app shell + skeleton.

t0_4.what: Definition: TTFB includes DNS, TCP/TLS, redirects, and server processing. It is the baseline for all other metrics — if TTFB is 1.5s, achieving LCP 2.5s is difficult.
t0_4.why: Frontend optimizations don’t help if the HTML itself arrives late. Slow DB queries, distant origin, redirects, and cold starts are the most common reasons.
cons: Requires coordination with the backend/infra team
gotchas: Redirect chains increase TTFB (http→https→www)
Cache hit vs miss yields different TTFB — measure both
Serverless cold starts create spikes
terms: Time from sending the request to receiving the first byte of the response. Target ≤ 800 ms.
Serving from a server close to the user to reduce latency.
The server/CDN responded without contacting the origin.

t0_5.what: Definition: There are two ways to measure performance: lab (Lighthouse, DevTools Performance panel) for debugging and field (CrUX, PageSpeed Insights, web-vitals JS library for RUM) for real user experience.
t0_5.why: Your laptop + fast WiFi and the user's mid-range phone are different worlds. Find the fix in the lab, then verify in the field that real users benefited.
pros: A complete picture from both lab and field
cons: Field data takes time to arrive (28-day rolling)
gotchas: Lighthouse scores and CrUX can differ
Apply CPU/network throttling in Chrome DevTools
The target is the 75th percentile, not the average
terms: Controlled test (Lighthouse, DevTools) — reproducible but synthetic.
Real users' data (CrUX, web-vitals library) — realistic.
Chrome User Experience Report: public field data, 28-day rolling.

t1_0.what:
Definition: A component re-renders when its state changes, its parent re-renders, or the context it reads changes. Re-render means the function runs again (render phase) — a DOM update is not required.

Even if props are the same, the child re-renders by default when the parent renders.
t1_0.why: Before optimizing you need a mental model: “Is the render slow?” or “Are there too many renders?” In most apps, the problem is keeping component state too high.
cons: Rendering semantics become slightly complex with concurrent features
gotchas: Re-render ≠ DOM update — React performs a diff
When the context value changes, all consumers re-render
Using index as key or inline objects causes unnecessary work
terms: State change, parent re-render, context value change.
Compute the diff between the new virtual tree and the old one to produce minimal DOM updates.
Objects/functions are newly created on each render, so they appear different for memoization.

t1_1.what: Definition: memo(Component) skips rendering if the props are the same as the previous render. However, if you create a new object/function on each render and pass it, the props are considered “changed” and memo becomes ineffective.
t1_1.why: Memo has its own cost (comparison + memory). It is beneficial only when the component is expensive and the props often remain the same. After the React Compiler arrives, the need for manual memo is reduced in many places.
gotchas: Inline {}, [], and arrow functions in props break memo
The children prop (JSX) is a new object on every render
Profile first, then apply memo
terms: Wraps a component: if props are shallow-equal, skip re-render.

t1_2.desc: Memoize expensive values (useMemo) and stable function references (useCallback). The real cost: memory + comparison overhead.
t1_2.what: Definition: useMemo(() => compute(a, b), [a, b]) caches the value; useCallback(fn, deps) caches the function (similar to useMemo(() => fn)). Both aim for referential stability or to save costly computation.
t1_2.why: They are not free: memory + dependency comparison. For most small calculations, the overhead outweighs the benefits. Correct usage: (1) give stable props to a memoized child, (2) need a stable function in hook dependencies, (3) when the calculation is truly expensive.
cons: Bugs from stale values when dependencies are incorrect
gotchas: useCallback does nothing on its own if the child is not memoized
All used values must be present in the deps array (follow lint rules)
If the compiler is on, you can often eliminate manual memoization
terms: Caches the result of an expensive calculation when dependencies do not change.
The value/function is recomputed only when this changes.

Look at not only render time but also commit/paint

t1_4.what: Definition: In a list of 10,000 rows, only ~20 visible rows are rendered; rows are reused on scroll. Libraries: react-window, @tanstack/react-virtual.
t1_4.why: If there are many DOM nodes, layout, paint, and memory all become slow. After 100+ complex rows, the benefit of virtualization becomes apparent.
cons: Ctrl+F, accessibility, dynamic heights and SEO are difficult
gotchas: Keep the item key stable, not the index
For variable height you need to measure and cache
Print/Ctrl+F cannot find offscreen rows
terms: Rendering only the visible rows in the DOM, not the rest.
Rendering extra rows just outside the viewport so scrolling feels smooth.
When rows have different heights, they need to be measured.

t1_5.desc: Mark state updates as non-urgent. The UI stays responsive during heavy re-renders. Concurrent rendering in practice.
t1_5.what: Definition: startTransition(() => setState(...)) tells React that this update can be interrupted. Urgent updates (input typing) are processed first and the heavy render runs later, the UI does not freeze.
t1_5.why: When typing in a search box, the render that filtered 10,000 items used to freeze the input. With a transition, the input updates immediately and the list updates later.
cons: The total work does not decrease, it is only prioritized
gotchas: Updates after async/await inside a transition are not tracked (use actions in React 19 for better handling)
Keep the state of a controlled input urgent
Memoize the heavy render as well; transition alone is not magic
terms: Marks a state update as non-urgent; provides isPending.
Typing/click is urgent; the heavy render for list filtering is a transition.
Provides a 'lagging' version of a value.

t2_0.what: Definition: rollup-plugin-visualizer, webpack-bundle-analyzer or vite-bundle-visualizer give a treemap of the build output. Large rectangles = large size. Start with the biggest segment first.
t2_0.why: Bundle size directly impacts parse/execute time and INP/LCP. Mistakes such as importing 'moment.js' or the whole lodash show up immediately in the treemap.
cons: Stats for gzip/brotli and parsed size differ — look at both
gotchas: Not just gzipped size; parsed size and execution time matter too
Deduplicate duplicate versions (peer dependencies)
Source maps make the analyzer more accurate
terms: Treemap that shows which library is adding how much JavaScript.
Multiple versions of a package in the bundle.
where: Choose lightweight alternatives instead of heavy dependencies.

t2_1.what: Definition: Perform route-based splitting first (separate each page into its own chunk). Then load heavy components (charts, editors, modals) on interaction. Prefetching the chunk makes the next navigation instant.
t2_1.why: The user shouldn't have to download the entire app's JavaScript for the first page. A smaller initial bundle = better FCP/LCP/INP.
cons: Risk of loading waterfalls and spinners
gotchas: Too many tiny chunks increase network overhead
A lazy component requires a Suspense boundary
Prefetch on hover/idle masks the delay
terms: Splitting the bundle into small chunks that load on demand.
import('./x') — returns a Promise, creates a separate chunk.
Load the component lazily and display a fallback.

t2_2.what: Definition: The bundler examines static ESM imports to determine which exports are unused and drops them. CommonJS is dynamic, so it is not shaken.
t2_2.why: Barrel files (index.ts that re-export everything) and side-effectful modules break tree shaking; the whole library gets included in the bundle.
cons: Because of side effects, the bundler stays on the safe side.
gotchas: List CSS imports in sideEffects, otherwise they may be dropped
export * and barrel files prevent shaking
Shaking does not occur in dev mode — check the production build
terms: The bundler removes unused exports from the final bundle.
Static import/export — can be analyzed; CommonJS require cannot.
Flag in package.json indicating that the module does not have side effects at import time.

t2_3.desc: Gzip vs Brotli (Brotli is 15-25% smaller). Static pre-compression vs on-the-fly. AVIF/WebP for images. woff2 for fonts.
t2_3.what: Definition: Text assets (HTML/CSS/JS/JSON/SVG) should be compressed with Brotli (or gzip). Pre-compress static files at build time (highest level); serve dynamic responses on the fly at a medium level. Browser Accept-Encoding sends, server replies with Content-Encoding.
t2_3.why: Network bytes are directly load time. Compression headers do not help for compressing images/video — change the format (AVIF/WebP).
cons: Max-level Brotli on the fly is CPU-heavy.
gotchas: Do not recompress already compressed files (jpg/mp4/woff2).
Vary: Accept-Encoding header is required for CDN.
Brotli is used by browsers only over HTTPS.
terms: 15–25% smaller compression than Gzip; best for text assets.
Create .br/.gz files at build time, server serves them directly.
Modern compressed formats for fonts and images.

t2_4.what: Definition: HTTP/2 multiplexing and header compression reduce the cost of many small files (unlike the 6-connection limit in HTTP/1.1). Server push is deprecated; use 103 Early Hints and resource hints instead.
t2_4.why: Place hints in the right spots: preload critical late-discovered resources, preconnect cross-origin API/CDN, prefetch the next page. Incorrect preload steals bandwidth.
cons: Too many hints dilute priority
gotchas: Preload without usage triggers a console warning and wastes bandwidth
Font preload requires crossorigin
Preconnect should be limited to 2–3 critical origins
terms: Multiple parallel requests on a single HTTP/2 connection.
preload = needed now (current page), prefetch = maybe on the next page.
Opening a connection to a third-party origin in advance.

t2_5.what: Definition: Strategy: HTML no-cache (validate each time), hashed static assets max-age=31536000, immutable, API/data stale-while-revalidate. Content-hashed filenames give a new URL on deployment, so cache invalidation is not needed.
t2_5.why: On repeat visits the network is completely avoided. Incorrect headers either show a stale site or waste the benefit of the cache.
gotchas: no-cache does not mean 'don’t cache', it means 'use after validation'
Don’t assign a long cache to HTML — a new deployment gets blocked
no-store can also block the bfcache
terms: Informs the browser/CDN how long to cache.

Serve the stale version immediately, refresh in the background.
cons: Invalidation planning is essential

t3_0.what: Definition: Modern formats: AVIF < WebP < JPEG in size. In <picture> provide AVIF, then WebP, then a JPEG fallback. Use AVIF/WebP for photos and SVG for logos/icons.
t3_0.why: Images make up a large portion of page bytes and LCP is often an image. Changing the format can be a bigger win than code optimization.
cons: Encode time and pipeline setup
gotchas: PNG/WebP lossless may be better for screenshots or flat graphics
Heavy compression can introduce artifacts
Auto-format and resize are easy with an image CDN
terms: Best compression, about 50% smaller than JPEG; encode slow.
Quality ~60–80 is often enough for visual match.

t3_1.what: Definition: srcset + sizes let the browser select the correct image based on the viewport and DPR. For art direction (different crop on mobile) the <picture> media source is used.
t3_1.why: Sending a 1x laptop image to a 3x phone wastes bandwidth; sending a small image to the phone looks blurry. The correct sizes give both performance and quality.
gotchas: sizes incorrect causes the browser to fetch a larger image
Provide both width and height — prevents CLS
Do not mix x and w descriptors in srcset
terms: How wide the image will appear in the layout (the browser selects based on this).
cons: Generating multiple variants (build/CDN)

t3_2.what: Definition: Apply loading="lazy" on below-the-fold images; on above-the-fold (especially LCP) image use eager (default) + fetchpriority="high". decoding="async" removes decoding from the main thread.
t3_2.why: Initial page weight is reduced. But making the LCP image lazy makes LCP very poor; this is the most common performance bug.
cons: Late load flicker can occur on scroll
gotchas: Do not apply lazy loading to the LCP image
Lazy images need width/height (to avoid CLS)
You need to consider preloading the next slides of a carousel
terms: Load offscreen images/iframes only when they approach the viewport.
Image decoding does not block the main thread.
For custom lazy loading or infinite scroll.

t3_3.desc: Inline above-the-fold CSS, defer non-critical CSS, remove unused CSS, PurgeCSS, critical npm package
t3_3.what: Definition: CSS is render-blocking. Inline the critical CSS, load the rest using the media="print" onload trick or preload asynchronously, and remove unused CSS with DevTools Coverage / PurgeCSS.
t3_3.why: A large stylesheet directly delays FCP/LCP. Frameworks with tools (Next, Astro) handle much of this automatically.
cons: Maintaining critical CSS and the risk of FOUC
gotchas: Inline CSS is not cached
Dynamic classes may be purged — provide a safelist
@import chains create a waterfall
terms: The minimum CSS required for above-the-fold rendering that is inlined in the head.
Rules that are not used on the page — found via a coverage tool.
Loading the remaining CSS in a non-blocking way.

t3_4.what: Definition: Serve fonts in woff2, subset them, preload critical fonts, and keep font-display: swap (or optional). Use a variable font to replace multiple weights with a single file.
t3_4.why: Fonts create render-blocking text (FOIT) or layout shift (FOUT swap). The system font stack is the fastest option.
cons: Effort required for subsetting and fallback tuning
gotchas: The crossorigin attribute is required in the preload
swap can cause CLS; use a metric-matched fallback
Self-hosting Google Fonts is often faster
terms: Only keep necessary characters (Latin) — smaller file.
Multiple weights/widths in a single file.

t3_5.what: Definition: Replace the animated GIF with <video autoplay muted loop playsinline>. Use preload="none" + poster on below-fold video. Animate only with transform/opacity.
t3_5.why: GIFs are very heavy and CPU-intensive. Video + poster reduces bytes and makes playback smooth.
cons: Autoplay policies (muted + playsinline required)
gotchas: Autoplay works only with muted video
Don't forget to provide a poster image
Don't apply will-change to everything
terms: MP4/WebM is 5–10× smaller than GIF; never use GIF.
Do not load the bytes of a below-fold video until it plays.

t4_1.what: Definition: Lighthouse runs on every PR via @lhci/cli, scores are compared, and a comment appears on the PR. In GitHub Actions, treosh/lighthouse-ci-action is common.
t4_1.why: It’s easy to forget to run Lighthouse manually. Running it in CI makes performance an automated quality gate, just like tests.

Keep test URLs representative and stable
Lab score field does not guarantee performance

t4_2.what: Definition: A service worker can intercept requests and serve them from the cache. Strategies: cache-first (static assets), network-first (API/HTML), stale-while-revalidate (feed, avatars). Offline fallback page and Background Sync (queued actions) are also possible.
t4_2.why: Repeat visits are instant, offline support and PWA features are provided. However, if update/invalidation is incorrect, users continue to see the old app.
cons: Debugging and update flow are complex
gotchas: On SW update, older tabs run the old version — plan skipWaiting/prompt
Only on HTTPS (localhost exempt)
Do not cache-first HTML without versioning

t4_3.what: Definition: Hydrating the entire page is heavy (TBT/INP suffer). Selective hydration (React Suspense), islands (Astro), and resumability (Qwik) provide interactivity with less JS. Hydrate below-fold components when idle/visible.
t4_3.why: SSR HTML appears quickly, but the page stays 'dead' until it is hydrated. Reducing hydration cost improves INP and TBT.
cons: Depends on architecture and framework
gotchas: Server/client HTML mismatches cause hydration errors
Sharing state between islands is difficult
Prerender ≠ interactive; avoid showing users a fake-interactive UI

t4_4.what: Definition: Third-party scripts affect the main thread, network, and CLS. Measure: Lighthouse 'reduce impact of third-party code', DevTools Network by domain. Fix: async/defer, lazy load, facades, Partytown, and Tag Manager audit.
t4_4.why: Often the biggest slowdown on a site isn’t your code, but the 15 scripts hidden inside the tag manager. Their impact isn’t visible without measurement.
cons: Tradeoff conversation with business teams
gotchas: A tag manager can load many scripts
Loading after consent still reduces the load
Self-hosting third-party scripts gives privacy and cache control, but updates become your responsibility

t4_5.desc: Sharing perf wins with the team. Automated regression detection. Grafana dashboards for RUM. Performance as a KPI.
t4_5.what: Definition: Performance culture = measurement + ownership. Dashboards (p75 LCP/INP/CLS by page), alerts on regressions, PR budgets, and share wins with business impact (e.g. 'LCP 400ms less → conversion +2%').
t4_5.why: One-time optimization slowly reverses over a few months. Culture and automation keep wins lasting.
cons: Effort for instrumentation and ownership
gotchas: Look at p75/p95, not averages
Segment by page/route
Linking wins to business metrics convinces stakeholders
terms: Show real users' vitals in Grafana/Datadog.
Automatic alert when metric exceeds threshold.
Tie performance to business metrics (conversion, bounce).
A maximum limit on a metric or size that makes the build fail.
t4_0.what: Definition: Budget = a limit: 'main JS ≤ 170KB gz', 'LCP ≤ 2.5s', 'CLS ≤ 0.1'. It is checked in CI; when a budget is broken the PR fails or warns.
t4_0.why: Performance degrades slowly (a little more JS in every PR). A budget stops regressions before they merge, and gives the team a shared target.
cons: Very tight budgets can slow the team down
gotchas: Keep realistic (data-based) budgets, not aspirational ones
Lab metrics are noisy — take the median of multiple runs
Review budgets over time
